title: Moving a box without arms, storing experience in text
lead: A snake robot pushes with its body, while another system reads notes from rehearsals. We explore how different methods help machines act and what the researchers actually tested.

news.title: A snake robot moves a box with its own body
news.summary: Northeastern University researchers showed a robot pushing a box without a separate arm. In 20 laboratory attempts, the box always finished within 20 centimetres of the target.
news.details: Northeastern University researchers in Boston presented COBRA, a snake robot that uses the same body for locomotion and pushing a box. It has no separate arm or permanently assigned object-contact section. A geometric planner sets approach and transport paths, while control software adjusts the direction of sidewinding motion. An external motion-capture system supplies robot and box pose. Autonomous action selection in this experiment therefore does not imply independence from laboratory tracking equipment.

news.body:
Moving an object need not start with gripping it between fingers. These researchers use the moving body itself: it rests on the floor and pushes the box through contact. The difficulty is that each bend changes both support and where force reaches the load. Planning must account for where the box will actually end up.

Northeastern University researchers in Boston presented COBRA, a snake robot that uses the same body for locomotion and pushing a box. It has no separate arm or permanently assigned object-contact section. A geometric planner sets approach and transport paths, while control software adjusts the direction of sidewinding motion. An external motion-capture system supplies robot and box pose. Autonomous action selection in this experiment therefore does not imply independence from laboratory tracking equipment.

The November 6 preprint describes 20 physical trials with different starting configurations and goals. All delivered the box within 20 centimetres of the target. That is the success threshold of a particular experiment on flat rigid ground, not a universal precision guarantee. The authors also model robot–ground and robot–box contact and separately test interaction optimisation in simulation. The full contact optimiser did not yet control the entire physical system in a closed feedback loop. Replacing external tracking with onboard sensing is identified as future work, alongside more integrated contact-aware control.

Another essential part sits outside the robot: equipment that tracks both machine and object. The reported system has not yet repeated this experiment without that external position measurement.

news.title: A robot reads practice notes without retraining its base model
news.summary: Huazhong University and ArcheOne AI describe RoboScript, which stores useful task steps in text memory. Its reported 83.4% average success concerns simulated two-arm tasks, rather than the same measured result on a physical robot.
news.details: Researchers at Huazhong University of Science and Technology and ArcheOne AI described RoboScript, a system that improves task execution by writing rehearsal feedback into text memory. The underlying model stays unchanged. Starting from one demonstration, it rehearses in simulation, records useful steps and object roles, and freezes that memory for evaluation on new scenes. The method is called World In-Context Learning: adaptation through information supplied alongside a task, rather than changes to the model's internal parameters.

The method is called World In-Context Learning: adaptation through information supplied alongside a task, rather than changes to the model's internal parameters.

If the available system struggles with a flexible cable or coordinating two arms, a better sentence does not by itself repair that skill. The authors' difficult cases mark a concrete boundary: information about the order of work and the physical ability to carry it out remain different things.
news.limitations: The 83.4% concerns simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, not physical trials. Rehearsals and existing movement skills are required; cloth, cables and close two-arm coordination remain difficult. Independent reproduction is not confirmed.
news.evidence_status: Research and author-run experiments; independent reproduction has not been confirmed.
news.organization: Huazhong University of Science and Technology; ArcheOne AI
news.body:
A robot's behaviour can change even when its underlying model is not retrained. Giving it different useful information can help, but somebody still has to obtain and test that information. In this work, notes emerge from practice in a computer world. The researchers separate experience of a particular task from the model parameters that process instructions and select actions.

Researchers at Huazhong University of Science and Technology and ArcheOne AI described RoboScript, a system that improves task execution by writing rehearsal feedback into text memory. The underlying model stays unchanged. Starting from one demonstration, it rehearses in simulation, records useful steps and object roles, and freezes that memory for evaluation on new scenes. The method is called World In-Context Learning: adaptation through information supplied alongside a task, rather than changes to the model's internal parameters.

The preprint appeared on November 9. Across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, a virtual suite of dual-arm manipulation, the authors report 83.4% mean success over clean and altered settings. Rehearsal and evaluation scenes are separated; memory is not rewritten for every test episode. Transfer to a physical dual-arm robot is also described, but 83.4% belongs to the virtual suite. Cloth, cables and tightly coordinated two-arm actions remain challenging. Leaving model parameters unchanged does not remove the cost of rehearsals, observations or the pre-existing movement skills used by the system.

A helpful note cannot supply a missing movement. If the available system struggles with a flexible cable or coordinating two arms, a better sentence does not by itself repair that skill. The authors' difficult cases mark a concrete boundary: information about the order of work and the physical ability to carry it out remain different things.

news.title: Google's new model controls robot arms and joins a factory pilot
news.summary: Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5, which turns images and verbal instructions into actions. A separate pilot with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz sorted parts at two operating factories, with a reported 96% task success rate.
news.details: Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5 on November 10, a model that chooses robot actions from images and verbal instructions. Its developer evaluated more than 200 distinct tasks, including tool use and flexible objects. A separate pilot with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz used Apollo 2 humanoids to pick metal automotive fastening parts, or brackets, from bins and place them in a required sequence. Trials took place on active production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. The company reports 96% task success for that pilot, without giving a total attempt count in the announcement.

news.body:
Seeing an object, processing an instruction and choosing a movement are different parts of handling things. The new model connects images, a verbal task and action. A factory system still extends beyond that model: it must also follow the sequence of work. Testing one skill in a laboratory and testing a complete configuration in production are different comparisons.

Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5 on November 10, a model that chooses robot actions from images and verbal instructions. Its developer evaluated more than 200 distinct tasks, including tool use and flexible objects. A separate pilot with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz used Apollo 2 humanoids to pick metal automotive fastening parts, or brackets, from bins and place them in a required sequence. Trials took place on active production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. The company reports 96% task success for that pilot, without giving a total attempt count in the announcement.

The system separates two levels: Gemini Robotics ER tracks the workflow, while the new action model controls the hands and arms. The production result therefore belongs to that configuration, rather than to one isolated neural network. Laboratory comparisons also vary by task: sweeping rubbish into a dustpan improved from 0% to 52% against Gemini Robotics 2, for example. The model is rolling out to robotics partners. These are developer-reported figures, without independent assessment, a complete human-intervention record or a cost per handled part in the release.

It is also a different operation. Its percentage cannot be pooled with 96% factory sorting to produce one overall rating for the robot.

news.title: Combining signals helps a robot stay on its feet
news.summary: The University of Michigan presented PRISM at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), an input-processing component for robot control networks. Simulated humanoids fell less often, while a separate physical-arm experiment tested picking up a roll of tape.
news.details: The University of Michigan presented PRISM at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin on November 10. It is an input component for a movement-control neural network. The preprint first appeared in July; the current event is its conference presentation, not a new original-publication date. PRISM learns useful multiplicative combinations of observations, previous actions and commands, such as joint-position and velocity signals. Replacing initial input processing lets it fit existing learning systems without a new training objective or extra sensors. Its contribution is a change in representation rather than simply a larger parameter count.

news.engineering_impact: Twenty-four seconds without falling is an understandable but limited test. It compares control variants under the same trial conditions, without telling us how many hours a machine will work in production. The physical arm tested an entirely different action, picking up a roll. The two results belong alongside each other, without either standing in for the other.
news.limitations: Research-team results from 24-second simulated walking trials and a separate 50-attempt physical grasp test. No independent reproduction or long-duration industrial evaluation is supplied; the preprint dates to July, with the conference presentation on November 10 being the new event.
news.evidence_status: Research and author-run experiments; independent reproduction has not been confirmed.
news.body:
Joint position and joint speed can be useful together as well as separately. Their interaction helps describe how motion changes. The researchers let the input section of a neural network learn useful combinations. This is not a new sense organ: it changes how available information is processed before the network produces a control action.

The University of Michigan presented PRISM at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin on November 10. It is an input component for a movement-control neural network. The preprint first appeared in July; the current event is its conference presentation, not a new original-publication date. PRISM learns useful multiplicative combinations of observations, previous actions and commands, such as joint-position and velocity signals. Replacing initial input processing lets it fit existing learning systems without a new training objective or extra sensors. Its contribution is a change in representation rather than simply a larger parameter count.

In simulation, humanoids completed 92.5% of 24-second trials without falling, against 51% for a conventional network. Enlarging the conventional network to a comparable size produced 52.3%. This measures stability over a fixed interval, not long-term service lifetime. In a separate physical test, an SO-101 arm picked up a roll of tape with 94% success across 50 attempts, against 68% using identical training demonstrations. The university reports its team's results. Simulated walking and physical grasping percentages belong to separate experiments, not one general reliability figure.

It compares control variants under the same trial conditions, without telling us how many hours a machine will work in production. The physical arm tested an entirely different action, picking up a roll. The two results belong alongside each other, without either standing in for the other.

news.title: Shared software development reaches a hospital delivery robot
news.summary: Mitsubishi Electric first applied its shared RoboPivot framework to software for MELDY, delivered to a Japanese hospital. Its reported 30% concerns estimated guidance-function development time, rather than the speed of hospital deliveries.
news.details: Mitsubishi Electric announced the first product application of RoboPivot on November 10. This shared software foundation supports robot development. Subsidiary Mitsubishi Electric Mobility used it for MELDY, a multipurpose hospital delivery robot supplied in November to St. Marianna University Hospital in Japan. Departments developed the foundation collaboratively inside the company, reusing code and experience instead of recreating similar functions. This is called InnerSource: open collaboration practices applied internally, rather than a promise that the entire codebase is publicly available.

Subsidiary Mitsubishi Electric Mobility used it for MELDY, a multipurpose hospital delivery robot supplied in November to St. Marianna University Hospital in Japan. Departments developed the foundation collaboratively inside the company, reusing code and experience instead of recreating similar functions. This is called InnerSource: open collaboration practices applied internally, rather than a promise that the entire codebase is publicly available.

news.limitations: The 30% is an estimate for guidance-function development including test-environment preparation. It does not measure delivery speed or hospital labour savings; absolute development time and independent evaluation are not supplied.

news.body:
A robot is more than a body and motors. Software determines behaviour, and developers need ways to test that behaviour. If colleagues have already built a similar component, it may be possible to use it again. This announcement follows that route: teams share their work inside a company, and the shared framework reaches a delivered product.

Mitsubishi Electric announced the first product application of RoboPivot on November 10. This shared software foundation supports robot development. Subsidiary Mitsubishi Electric Mobility used it for MELDY, a multipurpose hospital delivery robot supplied in November to St. Marianna University Hospital in Japan. Departments developed the foundation collaboratively inside the company, reusing code and experience instead of recreating similar functions. This is called InnerSource: open collaboration practices applied internally, rather than a promise that the entire codebase is publicly available.

The company estimates a 30% reduction in software-development lead time. A footnote defines the comparison: developing robot guidance functionality from scratch, including preparation of the verification environment. It does not measure travel speed, delivery volume or hospital staff time saved. A separate goal seeks a 50% reduction in the broader product-development cycle by 2030, with a different scope of comparison. Neither the absolute project duration nor independent verification of the estimated saving is supplied. The delivery announcement and the development estimate describe different outcomes.

Open collaboration here does not mean that any reader can download the robot's entire program. Sharing takes place inside the company. Nor does shorter software preparation tell us how many minutes a hospital delivery took. These are different clocks running in different parts of the work: the source estimates the first, without measuring the second.
